commitResults.messageTitle: Add getStartMessage() to the Game interface
commitResults.messageBody:
The main loop reads a line of input before it ever calls into the active
game, so a game had no way to display anything first. That is fine for
Wordle, which can wait for a guess, but the calculator game has to show
its first problem before the player can answer it.

Declare getStartMessage() as a default method returning an empty string
rather than an abstract one. A default method carries an implementation,
so WordleGame continues to compile untouched and future games opt in only
if they have opening text. The main loop prints the result after the
"Starting <game>..." line, skipping it when empty so existing games are
unaffected.

Part of #67.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Introduce the calculator game (feature F8, user story 10) as a Game
implementation with placeholder behaviour, so the class and its contract
land before the gameplay logic that follows.

Documents the passive-by-design decision on the class itself: handleInput()
takes one line and returns one response without looping or reading input,
keeping all cross-round state in fields. A game that owned the input loop
would lock the terminal into that game, which the product is not allowed
to do.

Part of #61.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add ArithmeticProblem, holding one generated problem and its answer, with the
operand ranges from the v1.0 UserGuide draft: 1-99 for addition and
subtraction, 2-12 for multiplication, and a 2-12 divisor with a 1-12 quotient
for division.

Two of the four operators need their operands constrained so the arithmetic
stays doable in the head. Subtraction orders the operands so the larger comes
first and the answer is never negative. Division works backwards from the
answer, building the dividend as divisor * quotient, so the result is always
a whole number -- generating a dividend first and dividing would mostly
produce fractions.

Instances are immutable and the constructor is private, so a problem can only
be produced by generate() and its answer cannot fall out of step with its
operands. The Random source is a parameter rather than a field created
internally, which is what makes generation seedable and therefore testable.

Operators are an enum rather than strings so the set is closed at compile
time and the switch can be checked for completeness.

Part of #62.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add answer checking and round feedback
commitResults.messageBody:
Grade the player's answer against the current problem and return feedback
immediately, then generate the next problem.

A wrong answer always reveals the correct one. The user guide calls for this
deliberately: the game is a drill, so a round the player got wrong should
still teach them the answer rather than just marking them down.

Implement getStartMessage() to show the first problem. The main loop reads a
line before calling into the game, so without this the player would be
staring at a prompt with no problem to answer.

Parsing goes through a helper that returns null instead of throwing, which
keeps the "not a number" case as ordinary control flow rather than an
exception. The regex accepts an optional leading minus sign per the guide,
and parseWholeNumber still catches NumberFormatException because a string of
digits can match the regex yet overflow an int.

Random is injected through a second constructor so tests can seed problem
generation and get repeatable problems; the single-argument constructor keeps
production code unchanged.

Part of #63.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Track and display round number and running score
commitResults.messageBody:
Add round, correct, and attempted counters, and open every round with a
header showing them:

  Round 3  |  Score: 1/2
    72 / 8 = ?

Score reads as correct/attempted. The two counters are kept separate rather
than derived from each other because they diverge: input that is not a whole
number is not an attempt, so attempted cannot simply be the round number
minus one.

The header is built in one helper used by both getStartMessage() and
handleInput(), so the opening round and every later round are formatted by
the same code and cannot drift apart.

reset() clears all three counters, otherwise a replayed session would start
with the previous session's score.

Expose the counters through getters so tests can assert on score without
parsing the display text.

Part of #65.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle non-numeric input without counting an attempt
commitResults.messageBody:
Input that is not a whole number now re-asks the same problem and leaves the
score untouched, with the message the user guide specifies:

    That is not a whole number. Try again - this round does not count.

The early return happens before any counter is touched, so a typo costs the
player nothing -- not an attempt, not a point, and not the problem they were
part way through working out. Generating a fresh problem here would be worse
than the score penalty, because it would throw away mental work the player
had already done.

Log the rejected input at FINE so the case is traceable without adding noise
to what the player sees, matching the logging style used in the main loop.

Part of #64.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Show a session summary when the player quits
commitResults.messageBody:
Typing 'quit' ends the session and reports rounds attempted, correct answers,
and accuracy as a whole-number percentage, then hands back to the main menu.

Accuracy shows as '-' rather than 0% when no rounds were attempted. A player
who quits immediately has no accuracy to report, and 0% would read as though
they had answered everything wrongly.

The round in progress when quit is typed is correctly excluded, because
attemptedCount only rises once an answer has been graded -- so the quit path
needs no special handling to honour that rule.

Checking for quit before parsing the input means the word is never mistaken
for an answer, and the check is case-insensitive and trimmed to match how the
rest of the application treats commands.

This also makes the game playable under the current main loop: quit is what
sets finished, which is the signal the loop waits on. Issue #69 will move
command routing up to the top level so that any command works mid-game.

Part of #66.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add CalculatorGame to the GameList constructor so it shows up in the game

commitResults.messageTitle: Add unit tests for the calculator game
commitResults.messageBody:
Add ArithmeticProblemTest and CalculatorGameTest, covering generation ranges,
grading, scoring, invalid input, quitting, accuracy, and reset.

Every test seeds its own Random so problems are repeatable. The range tests
generate 500 problems each rather than one: generation picks an operator at
random, so a single sample would pass even with a broken bound, while a few
hundred reliably exercises all four operators and both ends of each range.

Expected answers are read back from the game rather than hard-coded against
the seeded sequence. Hard-coded values would be testing a particular JDK's
Random implementation as much as the game, and would break if the generation
order ever changed. Wrong answers are produced by offsetting the correct one
by one, which is guaranteed wrong for any problem.

The range check for a division's dividend allows up to 144, since the
dividend is built as divisor * quotient and both top out at 12.

Part of #70.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Route all input through a single top-level command loop
commitResults.messageBody:
Remove the nested loop that ran a game to completion:

    while (!selectedGame.isFinished()) {
        ui.showMessage(selectedGame.handleInput(ui.readLine()));
    }

While that loop ran it owned the input stream, so every line went to the
active game and the launcher's own commands were unreachable. The player was
shut inside a game until it ended, which the product is not allowed to do.

The active game is now a variable in the one remaining loop. Each line is
checked against the launcher commands first, and only reaches the game if
none matched. So 'help', 'exit', and 'play' all work mid-game, and starting
a different game while one is running switches to it immediately.

This had no visible effect before now only because WordleGame sets finished
on every input, so the nested loop always ran exactly one iteration. The
calculator continues until the player leaves, which would have turned the
latent mode lock into a real one.

Supporting changes:

- Add Game.getExitMessage(), the counterpart to getStartMessage(), so a game
  can report a closing message when the launcher takes the player out of it
  rather than the game ending itself. Declared default so no existing game
  needs editing. CalculatorGame returns its session summary, shared with the
  'quit' path so both routes out report identically.
- Add GameList.findGameById() so the loop does not need to know how games are
  stored, replacing the inline search.
- Extract startGame() and showExitMessage() to keep the loop readable now
  that it handles switching between games.
- Ignore blank input instead of forwarding it, so pressing Enter during a
  game is not graded as an answer.
- Pass the raw line to handleInput() rather than the parsed command, since a
  game's input need not be a command at all -- the calculator wants a number.

Closes #69.
